chapters.title: Chapter 3: Corporate Tax Rates and Regimes

lessons.title: Minimum Alternate Tax: Why Profitable Companies Cannot Pay Zero Tax

body.text: A company can be genuinely profitable in its annual report and show almost no taxable income, entirely legally, by stacking up depreciation and incentives. Minimum alternate tax exists for exactly that company. It says: whatever your computation shows, pay at least a set percentage of the profit you told your shareholders about.

children.text: In the 1980s, a number of large listed Indian companies paid dividends out of healthy profits while paying no income tax at all. Nothing illegal had happened. Accelerated depreciation and investment incentives had simply wiped out their taxable income. The public reaction produced minimum alternate tax, and some version of it has been in the law ever since.

body.title: How minimum alternate tax got here

events.title: First version introduced
events.description: A minimum tax on book profits was brought in to catch profitable companies paying nothing, and was withdrawn a few years later.

events.title: Reintroduced and rebuilt
events.description: The provision returned and was recast into the book profit framework that companies recognised for the next two decades.

events.title: Rate cut to 15%
events.description: Alongside the new 22% concessional regime, the MAT rate fell from 18.5% to 15%, and companies opting into the concessional regime were taken out of MAT entirely.

events.title: Rate cut to 14%, and credit ends
events.description: The Finance Act, 2026 lowered the rate to 14% and made MAT a final tax in the old regime, so no new MAT credit is generated at all.

body.text: Read the second row again, because it is the quiet reason the 22% regime spread so fast. A company inside section 200 is not just paying a lower rate, it has stepped outside the minimum tax system altogether. There is no second computation, no book profit adjustment schedule and no credit tracking to maintain.

children.text: Book profit starts from the net profit in your audited profit and loss account, then moves in the opposite direction to the computation you built in Chapter 2. Tax depreciation, incentives and most disallowances play no part here. Instead, a short list of specified adjustments applies.

body.title: Two different starting points, two different destinations

children.text: The Change That Rewrote the Arithmetic

For twenty-five years, MAT was uncomfortable but survivable, because the excess came back. Pay MAT this year, build up a credit, and set it off in a later year when normal tax exceeded MAT. The company was lending money to the government, not losing it. The Finance Act, 2026 ended that.

body.caption: MAT credit before and after 1 April 2026

cells: Does paying MAT create a credit?
Yes, the excess over normal tax became credit
No. MAT in the old regime is a final tax
Can old accumulated credit be used?
Yes, against normal tax in later years
Only by a company in the concessional regime, capped at 25% of that year's tax liability
How long does old credit last?
15 tax years from the year it arose
The same 15-year limit continues to run
What about a company staying in the old regime?
Credit could be set off there
No set-off available in the old regime

body.text: This reverses a long-standing planning rule. Accumulated MAT credit used to be a reason to stay in the old regime, because switching to section 200 meant forfeiting it. Now the opposite is true: old credit can only be used by a company that has moved into the concessional regime, and only up to 25% of that year's tax liability. Any company still sitting on unused MAT credit should have this recomputed before its next return.

body.title: Try It: Compute the Floor
body.prompt: An old-regime company reports book profit of ₹8,00,00,000. Applying the 14% MAT rate with 7% surcharge and 4% cess, what is its minimum alternate tax? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: 14% of ₹8,00,00,000 is ₹1,12,00,000. Surcharge at 7% adds ₹7,84,000, giving ₹1,19,84,000, and 4% cess adds ₹4,79,360, for a total of ₹1,24,63,360 or about ₹124.63 lakh. That is an effective 15.5792% of book profit. If the company's normal tax came to less than this, ₹1,24,63,360 is what it pays, and under the current rules none of the excess comes back as credit.

body.title: Quick Check: Who Pays MAT?
body.question: Four companies each report large book profits and very low taxable income. Which one has to pay minimum alternate tax?
options: A software company that opted into section 200 [old 115BAA] two years ago
A textile company still in the old regime, claiming large incentive deductions
A new manufacturer taxed under section 201 [old 115BAB]
A company whose normal tax already exceeds 14% of its book profit
body.explanation: Only the old-regime company faces section 206 [old 115JB]. Companies inside the section 200 and section 201 regimes are outside MAT altogether, which is one of the quieter benefits of those regimes. The fourth company is technically within MAT but pays nothing extra, because MAT is a floor and its normal tax is already above it.

body.title: What about LLPs and partnership firms?

children.text: Non-corporate taxpayers have their own version, alternate minimum tax, now sitting in the same section 206 [old 115JC]. It applies at 18.5% of adjusted total income, which is taxable income increased by certain deductions claimed, and it bites only where those specific deductions have been claimed.

A straightforward LLP that claims no such deductions and simply pays 30% on its profit never encounters it. An LLP claiming profit-linked incentives should check the position each year, and should note that the consolidation of MAT and AMT into a single section has raised questions among practitioners about how widely it now reaches. This is a point to confirm with your accountant rather than assume.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Base MAT Uses
body.textWithBlank: Minimum alternate tax is charged not on taxable income but on ___ profit, taken from the accounts prepared under the Companies Act with specified adjustments.
body.explanation: Book profit. That is the whole design: the number a company shows its shareholders becomes the floor for the number it shows the tax department, so the two cannot drift too far apart without a cost.

body.title: Scenario: The Company That Planned for a Refund That Will Not Come
body.scenario: A Nashik auto components company has stayed in the old regime for years. It runs a heavy capital expenditure cycle, so tax depreciation keeps its taxable income low, and it has paid MAT in four of the last five years. Its board treats the accumulated ₹2.1 crore of MAT credit as money the company will recover once capital expenditure slows. It is now drawing up the budget for tax year 2026-27.
body.prompt: What should the finance team tell the board?
body.modelAnswer: Two things have changed, and both cut against the current plan. First, MAT in the old regime is now a final tax. From tax year 2026-27 this company will keep paying 14% of book profit plus surcharge and cess whenever that exceeds its normal tax, and none of the excess will build into credit any more. The comfortable idea that MAT is merely timing no longer holds, so every future year of heavy depreciation now carries a permanent cost rather than a deferred one. Second, the existing ₹2.1 crore of credit has not disappeared, but it can now be used only by a company that has moved into the concessional regime under section 200 [old 115BAA], and only up to 25% of that year's tax liability, within the original fifteen-year window. Staying in the old regime means that credit does nothing at all. The finance team should therefore model the switch properly: what the company pays on its full income at 25.168% with no incentive deductions, against what it pays in the old regime at 14% of book profit with no credit building up, and how quickly the ₹2.1 crore could be absorbed at 25% of each year's liability. For a capital-intensive company that has been trapped at the MAT floor for years, the arithmetic now usually points towards switching, but the option is irrevocable, so it deserves a five-year model and professional advice, not a board resolution based on last year's assumptions.

body.title: Annual MAT Review for an Old-Regime Company
steps: Compute both numbers every year: normal tax and 14% of book profit, each with surcharge and cess
Reconcile book profit to the audited profit and loss account, item by item, so the adjustments can be defended
Track how much accumulated MAT credit is left and how many of its fifteen years remain
Test whether moving to section 200 [old 115BAA] would let that credit be used, subject to the 25% cap
Re-run the regime comparison from the previous lesson with MAT treated as a permanent cost, not a timing one
Check whether an IFSC unit, if any, qualifies for the 9% rate
Have your accountant confirm the MAT report and computation before the return is filed

cards.definition: The single provision now holding both minimum alternate tax for companies and alternate minimum tax for non-corporates.
Net profit per the Companies Act accounts, with specified adjustments, used as the base for MAT.
14% of book profit from tax year 2026-27, an effective 15.5792% with 7% surcharge and 4% cess. IFSC units stay at 9%.
Tax that generates no credit and cannot be recovered later. MAT in the old regime became a final tax from 1 April 2026.
Excess of MAT over normal tax paid in earlier years, usable only in the concessional regime now, capped at 25% of the year's tax liability.
The non-corporate equivalent, at 18.5% of adjusted total income, triggered by claiming certain deductions.
Taxable income increased by the specific deductions that AMT is designed to claw back.

points: MAT under section 206 [old 115JB] makes a company pay at least 14% of book profit, whatever its taxable income shows
A company computes tax twice and pays the higher figure, with surcharge and cess applying to whichever wins
Companies inside the section 200 and section 201 regimes are outside MAT entirely
Book profit stays close to the audited accounts, with only specified adjustments, which is what makes the floor hard to avoid
From tax year 2026-27, MAT in the old regime is a final tax and generates no new credit
Accumulated credit from earlier years survives, but only a company in the concessional regime can use it, capped at 25% of that year's tax liability
Non-corporates claiming certain deductions face alternate minimum tax at 18.5% of adjusted total income

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. The MAT amendments made by the Finance Act, 2026 are recent, and their detailed application, particularly to accumulated credit and to non-corporate taxpayers, is still settling. Confirm the current position with a qualified chartered accountant before relying on it.
